replies.author: Kalaminator
replies.body:
What I'm interested on is how good AI is at following my specific instructions. AI is a tool to enhance your ideas, not a replacement. Any "one shot" game, no matter how cool it may look, will be dull, you have to give it purpose and intention. It can be a good base structure.

Let's say you give the same prompt to 2 different models, and you get different results. Are the result different because one model is better than the other? Could the other model with the right prompt and harness do something similar or better?, etc.

replies.author: GoodWilllPower
replies.body:
It’s also worth noting that one shotting can be impacted by what’s in your skills, memory and even proxy folders. 

I build a ton of apps and if I don’t start off a build in separate location from my existing apps when the build kicks off in an empty codebase you’ll notice one of the first things it does is review proxy folders. 

Not sure how this works with using Codex and Claude desktop given those have assigned files… but it’s a bad benchmark because these are all such massively different variables.

replies.author: Kalaminator
replies.body:
It doesn't make much sense. I explained to you why already. What makes a game fun is purpose and intention, a human who knows humans and what we enjoy. Sure, you can clone existing games, but AI didn't invent anything, still it will be a water down version. Sure you could create arcade style games, mini games, or filler style games.
Why would you ever want AI to take your place, when the fun is on making your own ideas come true? Unless you are proud thinking you achieved something by giving 4 prompts and having a dull, pointless game like many obviously are. There are millions of games out there, and people are not fan of AI, if you want anyone to play your game you better put good work into it and create something extremely cool, otherwise it will be more garbage to the pile.

comments.author: nberthdev
comments.body:
I have so many questions when I see posts like these. Assuming this really is a one-shot:

- How much did it cost to produce? How long did it take? How do those metrics compare to human output? Does using AI save money in this aspect?

- How many of the systems are direct copies of existing systems (e.g. AI used existing code). I'd assume all of them?

- Can we estimate the maintainability of the codebase? Could AI build new features on top of existing ones without breaking the game? What are the hidden costs of maintenance?

- Likewise: what kind of QA has been performed on the product? Was it performed by AI? What conclusions could we make of the initial state of the product?

And so on. It's amazing we have technology that does this, but I'm not sure I understand how useful and used it is in real development environments, and I want to understand it.
